# gup — Global Updater CLI (extended)

The long form of https://lindecker-charles.github.io/gup/llms.txt. Everything
below is generated from, or checked against, the repository at build time:
version @@VERSION@@, @@PROVIDERS@@ providers, Node.js >= @@NODE@@. Last content
change: @@MODIFIED@@.

Repository: https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup
Package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@@PACKAGE@@
Homepage: https://lindecker-charles.github.io/gup/
License: MIT

## One paragraph

On a developer machine, binaries arrive from dozens of competing sources and no
native tool covers them all: `winget upgrade --all` silently skips pinned
packages, `brew upgrade` never sees npm globals or VS Code extensions, `ncu -g`
only sees npm, and every cloud CLI ships its own `self-update`. `gup` is a
TypeScript CLI that unifies all of it: it shells out to each tool's own native
commands, fans out across providers with a bounded `p-limit(4)`, homogenises the
output, and answers one question first — *what is outdated, and from which
version to which version*. Updating is a separate, explicit step, run from a
full-screen terminal app that embeds the installers' own output. Windows, macOS
and Linux. MIT. No daemon, no telemetry; scheduled updates are opt-in and
started by the OS scheduler.

## Install and first run

```
@@INSTALL_COMMAND@@

gup doctor          # what was detected on this machine, and how to install the rest
gup list --fast     # what is outdated, skipping the slow providers
gup                 # full-screen interactive app
gup update --all -y # everything, no prompt (CI-safe)
```

Requires Node.js >= @@NODE@@. The package ships one bundled binary named `gup`.
Nothing runs until you run it — or until an opt-in schedule you created is
due, in which case the OS scheduler starts a short-lived gup process.

`--allow-scripts=node-pty` approves the install scripts of node-pty, gup's one
optional native dependency: the pseudo-terminal behind the embedded terminal
pane. npm 11 and later ask before running install scripts. Without the flag,
npm 11 runs them with a warning and npm 12 skips them — harmless on Windows and
macOS, which get a prebuilt binary, while on Linux the embedded terminal is then
unavailable and updates run in the plain terminal; with `strict-allow-scripts`
set, the install fails. To trust node-pty once for every global install:
`npm config set allow-scripts=node-pty --location=user`.

## Commands, flags and exit codes

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `gup` | Full-screen app (French UI): Scan · Paquets · Planification · Providers · Journal · Options · Quitter |
| `gup list` | Outdated packages as a table |
| `gup list --fast` | Skips providers marked `slow` (HTTP per package, filesystem walks) |
| `gup list --json` | Machine-readable array, pipeable |
| `gup list --provider <ids…>` | Restrict the scan to the given provider ids |
| `gup update` | Interactive multi-package selection, grouped by provider |
| `gup update --all` | Everything, after confirmation |
| `gup update --all -y` | Everything, no confirmation |
| `gup update <provider>:<packageId> …` | Surgical targets; bypasses the scan entirely |
| `gup doctor` | Detected providers, missing providers, install hints |
| `gup schedule` | List, add and run per-package scheduled updates |
| `gup report` | Activity journal as an offline HTML report, or `--format json|csv|text` |

Flags: `--fast` and `--provider <ids…>` on `gup list` and `gup update`;
`--json` on `gup list`; `-y` and `--timeout <seconds>` on `gup update`
(per-install wall clock; default 1200, `0` disables).
Environment: `GUP_INSTALL_TIMEOUT` (seconds; `--timeout` wins).

Exit codes: `0` success · `1` partial failure (at least one update failed) ·
`2` invalid arguments.

Full reference:
https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup/blob/main/docs/guide/cli-reference.md

## JSON output shape

`gup list --json` emits one object per provider:

```jsonc
[
  {
    "providerId": "brew",
    "available": true,
    "packages": [
      { "id": "ripgrep", "current": "14.1.0", "latest": "14.1.1" }
    ]
  }
]
```

A provider that failed carries `error: string` instead of throwing: the scan is
fail-soft, so one broken provider never takes the run down.

## The @@PROVIDERS@@ providers

One file per source under `src/providers/<domain>/`, no cross-imports, no shared
state. Each implements four methods: `isAvailable()`, `listOutdated()`,
`update()`, `updateAll()`. Ids below are the ones `provider:package` targeting
and `--provider` accept.

@@PROVIDER_INVENTORY@@

Per-provider status, notes and the roadmap of what is not covered yet:
https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup/blob/main/docs/guide/providers-catalog.md

## Platform support, precisely

**Windows** — the primary and historical target. OS-level: `winget`, `scoop`,
`choco`, plus `msys2`, `cygwin` and `npackd`. Plus the WSL bridge driven from
the Windows host (`wsl-apt`, `wsl-dnf`, `wsl-pacman`, `wsl-brew`,
`wsl-flatpak`, `wsl-nix`) and the WSL kernel itself (`wsl --update`).
Chocolatey upgrades go through a UAC elevation batch.

**macOS** — native since 0.3.0. OS-level: `brew` (formulae), `brew-cask`,
`macports`, `mas` (Mac App Store), plus `fink`, `sparkle` (apps that update
through Sparkle: reported, then left to the app's own updater) and the
cross-Unix `nix`, `pkgx` and `pkgin`. Homebrew installs a private prefix and only
exposes a PATH symlink, so `gup` resolves the link to its Cellar/Caskroom target
before classifying a binary — without that, every brew install was classified
`manual` and dropped from the scan. `--greedy` is deliberately omitted on casks:
apps marked `auto_updates true` update themselves on launch, and forcing the
cask upgrade re-downloads a whole bundle to reach a version the app would have
fetched anyway. `HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE` is inherited, never forced. Apple
Silicon and Intel.

**Linux** — `brew` and `nix` are the OS-level providers. Both are declared
`PLATFORMS.notWindows`, so Linuxbrew (`/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew`,
`~/.linuxbrew`) goes through the same code path as Homebrew on a Mac, and
native Nix gets the same two rows as on macOS (Nix itself and the user
profile; NixOS generations are out of scope). `pkgx` and `pkgin` run here too.
For a binary installed by the distribution, package databases are the only
reliable ownership signal, so `gup` probes `dpkg -S` / `rpm -qf` and delegates
that one package's upgrade to `apt` or `dnf`. There is no distro-wide `apt`,
`dnf`, `pacman` or `flatpak` provider on a native Linux host: those exist only
through the WSL bridge, declared Windows-only
(`readonly platforms = PLATFORMS.windows;`).

Everything above the OS layer is platform-independent: npm/pnpm/yarn/bun
globals, pip/pipx/uv/conda, cargo, rustup, gem, composer, dotnet tools, the
cloud/IaC/Kubernetes CLIs, VS Code and Cursor extensions, JetBrains IDEs,
pwsh modules, asdf/mise.

Of the @@PROVIDERS@@ providers, @@PROVIDERS_WINDOWS@@ run on Windows,
@@PROVIDERS_MACOS@@ on macOS and @@PROVIDERS_LINUX@@ on Linux. An OS-specific
provider declares the systems it supports (`PLATFORMS.windows`,
`PLATFORMS.macos` or `PLATFORMS.notWindows`); on any other system the registry
never probes, scans or updates it, and the Providers view and `gup doctor` list
it greyed out, as incompatible with the current OS. These per-system counts are
read from those declarations at build time.

## Architecture

- `src/cli.ts` — `commander` entry. Parses argv, routes to menu / list / update / doctor. No global state, no daemon.
- `src/core/registry.ts` — `ALL_PROVIDERS[]` plus `scanAll()`. The single place concurrency lives: `p-limit(4)`, with a `try/catch` inside each cell so no provider error propagates. `pLimit=4` keeps winget, scoop, choco, cargo and pipx from saturating the machine simultaneously.
- `src/core/runner.ts` — the one shell-out point. `execa` with an argv vector, UTF-8, `windowsHide`, never `shell: true`. The allowlist of executables is pinned by tests.
- `src/core/install-source.ts` — resolves who owns a binary (brew Cellar symlink, `dpkg -S`, `rpm -qf`, winget/scoop/choco paths) so the upgrade is delegated to the right manager instead of being reported as manual. Homebrew classification only accepts a `Cellar`/`Caskroom` segment under a known prefix, and `/usr/local` only in combination with such a segment — locked down by `tests/security/install-source.test.ts`.
- `src/core/wsl.ts` — the WSL bridge; `isWslAvailable()` returns false off win32.
- `src/providers/<domain>/<id>.ts` — one isolated module per source.
- `src/ui/**` — the full-screen OpenTUI app. Packages are checked with `space` (`a` for all) and updated with `enter` inside an OpenTUI embedded terminal (Ghostty VT core) fed by a pseudo-terminal, so installer prompts and progress bars work without leaving the interface. Updated packages then leave the list without a rescan. Where no pseudo-terminal is available (`node-pty` missing, `GUP_PTY=off`), the confirmation says why and the update runs in the plain terminal instead.

Lifecycle of a run: `isAvailable()` probes in parallel (`where`/`which`, milliseconds) → flags and filters are applied (`--fast` drops slow providers, `--provider` restricts the scan to the given ids) → `listOutdated()` fans out under `pLimit(4)` and `manual` packages are filtered once → selection → `runInherit()` streams stdout/stderr live, and every attempt is appended to the history log.

Reading order:
https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup/blob/main/docs/development/architecture.md then
https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup/blob/main/docs/development/how-gup-works.md

## Activity history (since 0.3.1)

Every scan and every update attempt is appended to a local JSONL log, one file
per calendar month, under the platform state directory:

```
%LOCALAPPDATA%\gup\history\YYYY-MM.jsonl                    # Windows
~/Library/Application Support/gup/history/YYYY-MM.jsonl     # macOS
$XDG_STATE_HOME/gup/history/YYYY-MM.jsonl                   # Linux (default ~/.local/state)
```

```jsonc
{"v":1,"ts":"…","runId":"…","gup":"@@VERSION@@","platform":"win32","kind":"scan",
 "durationMs":8421,"fast":false,"filter":[],"outdated":7,
 "providers":[{"providerId":"winget","outdated":5},{"providerId":"npm-g","outdated":2}]}
{"v":1,"ts":"…","runId":"…","gup":"@@VERSION@@","platform":"win32","kind":"update",
 "providerId":"npm-g","packageId":"typescript","status":"success",
 "from":"5.9.2","to":"6.0.3","durationMs":14108}
```

JSONL rather than a JSON array or a database: one self-describing object per
line makes an append a single `write`, so an elevated child and its parent can
log concurrently without a lock, and a process killed mid-write costs one line
instead of the file. The Journal view reads it back (activity and
most-updated-package charts in the terminal), and `gup report` renders it as a
single offline HTML file, or exports it as JSON or CSV.

## Security model

- Subprocess execution goes through one point, in a strict argv vector. `shell: true` is never used. The executable allowlist is pinned by tests.
- Network access is HTTPS-only: providers' version checks, plus the GitHub release archives the Windows-only `nerd-fonts` provider downloads and installs. No telemetry, ever.
- CI on every commit: CodeQL `security-extended`, Semgrep (`p/typescript` + `p/nodejs`), gitleaks, `audit-ci`, `eslint-plugin-security`, plus a Vitest suite dedicated to the security invariants. Dependabot runs weekly.
- Destructive actions are opt-in. `--all` asks before it acts unless `-y` is passed.

Threat model and disclosure process:
https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup/blob/main/SECURITY.md

## What gup deliberately does NOT do

- It does not replace winget/brew/npm/pip. It orchestrates their native commands.
- It is not a registry or a cache, and downloads nothing it installs itself — except Nerd Fonts on Windows, whose `nerd-fonts` provider fetches the font families' release archives.
- It does not resolve project manifests: no `package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `pom.xml`, `Gemfile`. Global installs only.
- It does not update the OS: Windows Update (use `PSWindowsUpdate`) and macOS `softwareupdate` are out of scope.
- It does not touch Maven / Gradle / sbt / bundler / lockfiles.
- It does not manage JetBrains Toolbox-installed IDEs (Toolbox ships its own updater).
- It runs no daemon. Opt-in scheduled updates register one OS scheduled task (Task Scheduler, launchd or cron) that starts a short-lived check; nothing stays resident.

Rationale: https://github.com/LINDECKER-Charles/gup/blob/main/docs/guide/scope.md

## Frequently asked, answered

**Does gup replace my package managers?** No. It calls their native commands and
homogenises the output.

**Does it work on macOS?** Yes, natively since 0.3.0 — Homebrew formulae and
casks, MacPorts, and the Mac App Store through `mas`.

**Does it work on Linux?** Yes. Homebrew/Linuxbrew and Nix cover the OS level,
and distro-owned binaries are upgraded through `apt`/`dnf` after ownership is
resolved with `dpkg -S` / `rpm -qf`. Full `apt`/`dnf`/`pacman`/`flatpak`
providers exist only via the WSL bridge from a Windows host.

**Can I use it in CI?** Yes. `gup list --json --fast` is machine-readable,
`gup update --all -y` skips every prompt, and the exit codes are stable.

**How is it different from topgrade?** topgrade runs the updates; gup starts by
telling you what is outstanding and from which version to which version, as a
separate phase, with JSON output, per-package selection, `provider:package`
targeting that bypasses the scan, and a local history of what it did. gup is
TypeScript on npm and covers @@PROVIDERS@@ sources including editor extensions
and JetBrains IDEs.

**Is it safe to let it update everything?** Updating is always explicit. `--all`
confirms unless `-y` is passed, `gup list` never writes anything, and the
shell-out layer is argv-only with a test-pinned allowlist.
